title: The Lion of Judah Began Here
paragraphs:
The Lion of Judah Began Here
Before There Was a Crown, There Was a Scandal. Before There Was a Throne, There Was Grace. Before the Lion Roared, God Was Already Rewriting Everything.

If someone handed you a family tree and asked you to guess who would become the greatest King in history, you probably wouldn't stop at the names stained by failure. You would skip the adulterers, the liars, the prostitutes, the foreigners, the broken fathers, the grieving mothers, and the families marked by betrayal. We naturally look for polished beginnings because we assume greatness must come from greatness.
God does the opposite.
He intentionally shines His light on the people we would rather erase.
The story of the Lion of Judah does not begin with perfection.
It begins with grace.
That should stop every one of us in our tracks.
Because if the Lion of Judah began with grace, maybe your story can too.
The title "Lion of Judah" first emerges in Jacob's prophetic blessing over his sons shortly before his death. Speaking under God's providence, Jacob declared over Judah:

"Judah, you are he whom your brothers shall praise... Judah is a lion's cub... The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until Shiloh comes; and to Him shall be the obedience of the peoples." (Genesis 49:8–10)
The Hebrew text is breathtaking.

"גּוּר אַרְיֵה יְהוּדָה"
Gur Aryeh Yehudah.
Literally:
"A young lion is Judah."

The word גּוּר (gur) refers to a lion cub—not yet fully grown, but already possessing the nature of a lion. The prophecy wasn't merely describing Judah's tribe; it pointed forward to a King whose authority would never end.
Jacob also declared:
"לֹא־יָסוּר שֵׁבֶט מִיהוּדָה"
"Lo-yasur shevet miYehudah."
"The scepter shall not depart from Judah."
The word שֵׁבֶט (shevet) means scepter, rod, or kingly authority. God was promising an everlasting royal line long before Israel ever had its first earthly king.
Centuries later, this promise would find its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
The Apostle John records Heaven's announcement in Revelation 5:5:
"Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered."
In Greek:

Ἰδοὺ ἐνίκησεν ὁ λέων ὁ ἐκ τῆς φυλῆς Ἰούδα
Idou enikēsen ho leōn ho ek tēs phylēs Iouda.
"The Lion from the tribe of Judah has overcome."

The word λέων (leōn) means lion—a symbol of royal authority, strength, majesty, and victorious power. Yet what John sees next overturns every human expectation. He hears about a Lion, but when he looks, he sees "a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain" (Revelation 5:6). The conquering Lion reigns through the sacrificial Lamb. Jesus wins not by worldly force but by His atoning death and triumphant resurrection.
The Lion and the Lamb are the same Savior.
That is the Gospel.
But before Judah became associated with kingship, something else happened.
Something most people wish wasn't in the Bible.
Genesis 38 interrupts the story of Joseph with what seems like an uncomfortable detour.
Judah.
Tamar.
Failure.
Deception.
Shame.

Judah failed to keep his promise to Tamar, his widowed daughter-in-law, by withholding his son Shelah. Tamar, seeking justice within the customs of that time, disguised herself, and Judah unknowingly fathered children through her. When the truth came to light, Judah confessed:
"She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah." (Genesis 38:26)
The Hebrew says:

צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי
Tzadeqah mimmeni.
"She is more righteous than I."
This was not Judah declaring Tamar sinless. It was a confession that he had failed in his covenant responsibility. For the first time, Judah publicly acknowledged his own guilt instead of hiding it.
Repentance began where excuses ended.
And remarkably, from Perez—the son born through this painful account—came the royal line that led to King David and ultimately to Jesus the Messiah (Matthew 1:3–16).

God did not endorse Judah's sin. Scripture consistently presents sin as rebellion against God. Yet in His sovereign grace, He redeemed what human sin had broken and wove it into His redemptive plan. That is not approval of evil; it is the triumph of God's mercy over human failure.
How many of us spend our lives trying to erase the chapters God has already forgiven?
How many believers secretly think their worst mistake permanently disqualified them from being used by God?
We hide.
We pretend.
We smile in church while carrying silent shame.
We assume God only writes beautiful stories with beautiful people.
But Scripture refuses to let us believe that lie.
Look carefully at Jesus' genealogy in Matthew 1.
Tamar is there.
Rahab is there.
Ruth is there.
Bathsheba is there, introduced as "the wife of Uriah," reminding us of David's grievous sin.
None of these names appear to glorify sin. They testify to the God who redeems sinners. Matthew does not sanitize history because the Gospel is not built on human perfection but on divine grace.
That doesn't minimize sin; it magnifies the mercy of Christ.
The Lion of Judah did not emerge from an immaculate human lineage.
He entered a broken family to rescue broken families.
He entered a sinful world to save sinners.
He entered our darkness because we could never climb into His light on our own.
This is why the Gospel never begins with, "Become good enough."
It begins with, "Christ died for the ungodly" (Romans 5:6).
The Lion roars not to terrify those who repent, but to declare victory over sin, death, and Satan. He calls people not merely to admire Him, but to turn from sin and trust Him as Lord and Savior.
Maybe you've convinced yourself that your failures are too many.
Maybe you've replayed your regrets until they became your identity.
Maybe you're exhausted from trying to prove you're worthy of God's love.
Listen carefully.
The Lion of Judah did not come looking for flawless people.
He came to seek and save the lost.
Your past may explain where you've been, but it does not have the authority to define who you become in Christ.
If you have repented and placed your faith in Jesus Christ, your identity is no longer anchored in your worst chapter. It is anchored in the finished work of the cross and the empty tomb.
That is why our mission has always been simple:
This isn't a slogan.
It's the testimony of Scripture from Genesis to Revelation.
It's Judah.
It's David.
It's Peter.
It's Paul.
It's every believer who has been rescued by the grace of God through faith in Christ.
If this message reminded you that God's grace is greater than your past, don't let it stop with you. Your testimony may be the encouragement another believer needs today.
One day, every earthly story will fade.
Only the story Jesus rewrote by His grace will remain.
